questions.question: In the following number-pairs, the second number is obtained by applying certain mathematical operation(s) to the first number. Which numbers should replace X and Y, so that the pattern followed by the two numbers on the left side of :: is the same as that on the right side of ::? (NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 – Operations on 13 such as adding to/subtracting from/multiplying with 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.) X : 126 :: 21 : Y
questions.questionHtml:
In the following number-pairs, the second number is obtained by applying certain mathematical operation(s) to the first number. Which numbers should replace X and Y, so that the pattern followed by the two numbers on the left side of :: is the same as that on the right side of ::?

(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 – Operations on 13 such as adding to/subtracting from/multiplying with 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.)

X : 126 :: 21 : Y
questions.solution:
Solution:

Given pattern: X : 126 :: 21 : Y

Try option (c): X = 12

Check relation:
12 × 9 + 18 = 108 + 18 = 126 ✔

Apply same rule to 21:
21 × 9 + 18 = 189 + 18 = 207 ✔

Hence, the pattern is number × 9 + 18

questions.question: Read the given statement(s) and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statement(s). Statements: Some pencils are swans. No vultures are pencils. Conclusions: (I) No vultures are swans. (II) Some swans are not vultures.
questions.questionHtml:
Read the given statement(s) and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statement(s).
Statements:
Some pencils are swans.
No vultures are pencils.
Conclusions:
(I) No vultures are swans.
(II) Some swans are not vultures.
questions.solution:
Answer: Only conclusion (II) follows.

Short Solution:
Some pencils are swans, and no vultures are pencils. So, the swans that are pencils cannot be vultures. Hence, some swans are not vultures (Conclusion II) is correct.

However, we cannot say that no vultures are swans, because not all swans are pencils. So, Conclusion I does not follow.

questions.solution:
Statement I says: I is taller than M but shorter than D.

It also mentions I is shorter than only one pole, meaning exactly one pole is taller than I.

From this, D must be the tallest pole as it is taller than I, and I is second tallest.

Thus, statement I alone is sufficient to find the tallest pole, which is D.

Statement II says: M is taller than L.

This information does not help determine the tallest pole alone or add conclusive information to statement I.

Therefore, statement II alone is insufficient and combined does not add value beyond statement I.

Hence, the answer is option 1.

questions.question: Read the given statement(s) and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statement(s). Statements: All kings are bombs. No parrots are kings. Conclusions: (I) Some bombs are not parrots. (II) Some bombs are kings.
questions.questionHtml:
Read the given statement(s) and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statement(s).
Statements:
All kings are bombs.
No parrots are kings.
Conclusions:
(I) Some bombs are not parrots.
(II) Some bombs are kings.
questions.solution:
Answer: Both conclusions (I) and (II) follow.

All kings are bombs, so kings are a subset of bombs. Also, no parrots are kings, so kings are completely separate from parrots.

Thus, the kings (which are bombs) are not parrots ⇒ some bombs are not parrots (I) follows.
Also, since all kings are bombs, clearly some bombs are kings (II) follows.

questions.question: Refer to the given number, symbol series and answer the question that follows. Counting to be done from left to right only. (All numbers are single digit numbers only) (Left) 6 £ 2 @ % 7 8 # 1 3 * 9 $ & 4 ^ ≺ 5 (Right) How many such symbols are there each of which is immediately preceded by an odd number but not immediately followed by an even number?
questions.questionHtml:
Refer to the given number, symbol series and answer the question that follows. Counting to be done from left to right only. (All numbers are single digit numbers only)
(Left) 6 £ 2 @ % 7 8 # 1 3 * 9 $ & 4 ^ ≺ 5 (Right)
How many such symbols are there each of which is immediately preceded by an odd number but not immediately followed by an even number?
questions.solution:
The series is 6 £ 2 @ % 7 8 # 1 3 × 9 $ & 4 ^ ≺ 5.

We check each symbol's immediate neighbours:

Identify symbols preceded by an odd number (1,3,5,7,9) and not followed by an even number (0,2,4,6,8).

Symbols preceded by odd numbers:

After 7: % (preceded by 7, next symbol 8 even) → Not counted

After 1: 3 (number, skip)

After 3: × (preceded by 3 odd, next symbol 9 odd) → Count 1

After 9: $ (preceded by 9 odd, next symbol & symbol) → Count 2

After 5: No symbol after 5 (end of series) so no symbol after this

Check symbols immediately preceded by odd number and not immediately followed by even number: × and $.

Total such symbols = 2.

Final answer: Option 4

(I) Nitin is sitting immediately to the right of Mehul.

(II) Prakash is sitting immediately to the left of Sandeep.

questions.solution:
Explanation:

Statement I tells us that Nitin is immediately to the right of Mehul , but this alone does not indicate who is at the extreme left , so it is insufficient .

Statement II tells us that Prakash is immediately to the left of Sandeep , but this alone also does not reveal the extreme left person , so it is insufficient.

Combining both statements, we have information about adjacent pairs (Mehul–Nitin and Prakash–Sandeep), but we cannot determine the full order of all four people . Therefore, even together, the extreme left person cannot be identified .

Answer: Data in both statements I and II together are NOT sufficient to answer the question.
